\chapter{Colours}
\label{ch:ta-colours}
\hlchaptermodality{11}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name black, white, red, and blue in Tamil and say which three are native and which one is the Sanskrit loan.}

Say karuppu, veḷḷai and sivappu as the native three, nīlam as the borrowed one, and hear veḷḷai echo veḷḷi from last chapter.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ta{கருப்பு} \ta{வெள்ளை} \ta{சிவப்பு} \ta{நீலம்}]{\ta{கருப்பு}, \ta{வெள்ளை}, \ta{சிவப்பு}, \ta{நீலம்} — three of Tamil's own, one borrowed}

\label{lesson:TA-C11-nirangal}



\begin{quote}
You've already seen Tamil mix native and Sanskrit words in its day-names. Colors tell a \textbf{cleaner} version of the same story: three colors are Tamil's own, and the fourth is the one color that keeps showing up borrowed, in language after language.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ta{கருப்பு}} (\emph{karuppu}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{black}\textquotedblright{} — native Tamil/Dravidian.
  \item \textbf{\ta{வெள்ளை}} (\emph{veḷḷai}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{white}\textquotedblright{} — native Tamil/Dravidian, and built on the very same \textbf{\ta{வெள்}} (\emph{veḷ-}, \textquotedblleft{}bright, silvery\textquotedblright{}) root you already met in \textbf{\ta{வெள்ளி}} (\emph{veḷḷi}), \textquotedblleft{}Venus/silver,\textquotedblright{} from the days-of-the-week lesson.
  \item \textbf{\ta{சிவப்பு}} (\emph{sivappu}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{red}\textquotedblright{} — native Tamil/Dravidian.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{நீலம்}} (\emph{nīlam}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{blue}\textquotedblright{} — from \textbf{Sanskrit} \ta{நீல} (\emph{nīla}), \textquotedblleft{}dark blue,\textquotedblright{} the very same root behind Hindi's \textbf{\dv{नीला}} (\emph{nīlā}). This \emph{nīla} is also the name of the indigo plant and its dye — part of why blue dye is so historically linked to India — but be careful: the English word \textbf{indigo} itself is a \emph{separate}, Greek-derived word (describing where the dye was imported \emph{from}, not descended from \emph{nīla} by sound change; see the Hindi color lesson for that careful distinction).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
This isn't random. \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Blue\textquotedblright{}} is, across many of the world's languages, one of the \textbf{last} basic colors to settle into its own fixed word — often arriving late, or borrowed, compared to black, white, and red. Tamil's colors look like exactly this pattern in miniature: three old, native words, and one — blue — reaching outside the language for a Sanskrit loan.

(Note for the Tamil-speaking reviewer: please confirm \emph{karuppu, veḷḷai, sivappu, nīlam} are the forms you'd teach first — regional/colloquial Tamil may prefer different everyday variants, and this lesson would benefit from your check the way the day-names lesson did.)
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three native ones — \textquotedblleft{}karuppu, veḷḷai, sivappu\textquotedblright{} — black, white, red
  \item the borrowed one — \textquotedblleft{}nīlam\textquotedblright{} — blue, from Sanskrit
  \item the echo — \textquotedblleft{}veḷḷai\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}veḷḷi\textquotedblright{} share the same veḷ- root
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which three Tamil colors are native, and which one is borrowed? (\textbf{Karuppu, veḷḷai, sivappu} (black/white/red) are native; \textbf{nīlam} (blue) is a \textbf{Sanskrit} loan.) What root does \emph{veḷḷai} share with a word you already know? (\textbf{Veḷ-} \textquotedblleft{}bright/silvery\textquotedblright{} — the same root as \emph{veḷḷi}, \textquotedblleft{}Venus/silver.\textquotedblright{}) Why might blue be the one borrowed color? (\textbf{Blue is often one of the last basic colors} to settle into a fixed word across many languages — the same pattern Latin's \emph{caeruleus} showed.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[llla]{\ta{ழ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TA-S115-letter-llla}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ta{◌ா} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{ழ}}
\textbf{\ta{ழ}} — \emph{llla}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{lll}, it is \textbf{llla}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \ta{ழ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ta{தமிழ்} \ta{எழுத்து}} \emph{tamiḻ eḻuttu} — why Tamil writing is so round
  \item \textbf{\ta{நான்} \ta{தமிழ்} \ta{பேசுகிறேன்}} \emph{nāṉ tamiḻ pēsugiṟēṉ} — I speak Tamil
  \item \textbf{\ta{வாழ்}} \emph{vāḻ} — to live, to flourish
  \item \textbf{\ta{எனக்குத்} \ta{தமிழ்} \ta{தெரியும்}} \emph{enakkut tamiḻ teriyum} — 'I know Tamil'
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \ta{ழ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ta{ழ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ta{ழ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ta{வணக்கம்}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ta{ழ} three times, saying \emph{llla} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \ta{ழ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ta{ழ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{llla}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
